title: Built with Claude: A Minecraft Mod to Intelligently Resolve Conflicts Between Structure Mods (No More Brute-Forcing!)

**Structure Arbiter Mod**  
[**https://www.curseforge.com/minecraft/mc-mods/structures-arbiter**](https://www.curseforge.com/minecraft/mc-mods/structures-arbiter)

**Structure Arbiter: Deterministic Pre-Generation Arbitration of Overlapping Structures**

Structure Arbiter addresses a failure mode that arises when many mods contribute structures to the same world: each mod decides placement independently, so two structures may be assigned overlapping volumes, and whichever generates later overwrites the other. Rather than altering terrain or the structures themselves, the mod intervenes at the single point where a structure’s footprint becomes known but nothing has yet been written to a chunk. It hooks `ChunkGenerator#tryGenerateStructure` with a Mixin that redirects the call to `Structure#generate`. The resulting `StructureStart` already carries the bounding box of the structure’s pieces, and this box is treated as the structure’s declared intent: a spatial claim that is independent of the blocks the structure would eventually place. The claim is compared against the claims of neighbouring structures, and the structure is either allowed to proceed unchanged or discarded by returning an empty `StructureStart`, so that nothing is placed.

The arbitration rule is a priority-ordered greedy procedure over a conflict relation. Two claims conflict when their three-dimensional boxes intersect after the horizontal extent of one is inflated by a margin, which defaults to eight blocks and accounts for terrain adaptation that spills beyond a structure’s nominal bounds; because the test is volumetric, a structure deep underground does not conflict with one on the surface. Claims are totally ordered by priority and then by structure identifier, which are both known before the structure is generated. Under the default configuration all priorities are equal, so the lexicographic order of identifiers decides ties, and priorities can be overridden per structure through the mod’s API. A structure survives if and only if its box does not conflict with the final placement of any higher-ranked structure in its neighbourhood. Determining those final placements is recursive, since a higher-ranked neighbour may itself have been displaced by a still higher-ranked one, but because rank strictly decreases along every dependency the recursion always terminates. Instances of the same structure never contest each other, since their spacing is already governed by the owning mod’s placement rules, and exempting them prevents densely distributed small structures from being rejected in bulk by their own siblings.

The central design property is that the outcome for any structure is a pure function of the world seed, the structure’s own claim, and the set of structures that the registered placement rules would generate nearby. Nothing depends on which chunks have already been generated, on the order in which a player explores the world, on thread scheduling, or on mod load order. To evaluate a decision, the mod must know the claims of neighbouring structures without generating their chunks, so it reconstructs them on demand: for every registered random-spread structure set it enumerates the candidate chunks inside a window around the structure under evaluation, using the same placement function that vanilla uses, and it runs `Structure#generate` for those candidates on a detached height accessor, discarding the result after reading its bounding box. Because generation is deterministic in the seed and chunk coordinates, the reconstructed claim is identical to the one that will eventually be produced when that neighbouring chunk is actually generated. Decisions and reconstructed claims are cached, and concurrent requests for the same candidate are coalesced so that only one worker thread performs the work.

Reconstruction by generation is expensive, because jigsaw structures assemble their pieces by trial and error, and the cost of a naive implementation grows with the area scanned multiplied by the number of structure sets across all installed mods. The mod therefore discards candidates as early and as cheaply as possible, in a fixed order. Whole structure sets are excluded once at start-up if they are not random-spread, if their spacing falls below a configurable threshold (dense, small features such as monster rooms), or if the user has excluded their namespace or identifier. Within a query, candidates that cannot reach the window given a configurable maximum structure extent are skipped, as are candidates that rank below the structure being decided or share its identifier, since neither can influence the result and both are recognisable from the identifier and priority alone. Finally, because vanilla evaluates biome validity only after the costly piece assembly, a biome pre-filter samples the biome source at the candidate chunk centre at several heights and skips generation if no sampled biome is permitted. The first three of these filters are exact with respect to the decision, and the solver independently re-applies the rank filter so that its results do not rely on the source honouring it; the extent bound and the biome pre-filter are approximations that can cause an overlap to go undetected but never cause a structure to be rejected incorrectly.

The solver supports displacing a conflicting structure along a deterministic, seed-derived sequence of candidate offsets before giving up, but the default maximum shift is zero, so by default a structure that loses a conflict is rejected rather than moved. After a rejection, vanilla’s own selection loop proceeds to the next weighted entry of the same structure set, which means a smaller variant may be placed where a larger one was refused. The mod records every decision together with the higher-ranked structures that blocked it, and exposes aggregate statistics, per-structure lookahead cost, and a listing of the structures around the player through the `/arbiter` command, so that heavy structures can be identified and excluded.

The approach has stated limits. Only random-spread placements are arbitrated, so ring-placed structures such as strongholds are outside its scope, as is any content that writes blocks through code other than the structure system. All entries of a multi-entry structure set are treated as potential claims even though only one is eventually selected, which makes the arbitration conservative. Conflicts with structures larger than the configured extent can be missed. Determinism and the absence of residual overlaps have been verified by randomized tests of the solver in isolation, covering order independence, locality, and pairwise non-overlap, while the integration with the game’s generation pipeline has been observed in practice on a modded world rather than proven.
